subject: vampire moth
title: A Moth Drills Into Skin and Drinks Blood for 50 Minutes. Only Males Do

scenes.text: Some moths drink blood. Only the males, and nobody knows why.
The vampire moths of Asia and Eastern Europe have a tongue lined with hooks and barbs, built for stabbing into fruit.
Some populations turned that tool on animals, and people. The moth rocks its head back and forth to drill the tongue in.
Then the hooks open to anchor it, and it drinks. One feed can last up to 50 minutes.
Of 17 species, eight have been seen drinking mammal blood. In Russia, one population was offered human hands and bit.
Females never do it. The best guess: the males collect salt from the blood and pass it to females as a gift when they mate.

description:
Moths of the genus Calyptra, the vampire moths, have a hooked, barbed proboscis evolved for piercing fruit. In parts of Asia, Africa and Eastern Europe, males use it to pierce the skin of mammals, including people, and drink blood for up to 50 minutes.
Eight of the 17 species have been recorded blood-feeding in the wild, and a Russian population of Calyptra thalictri fed on human hands in field experiments led by entomologist Jennifer Zaspel. Only males feed on blood; the leading hypothesis is that they pass the salt to females during mating.
Would you let a moth bite you for science? Comment below.
first_comment: The first confirmed bite on a scientist happened in 2006, when a moth in a collecting vial pierced her thumb. Which blood-drinking animal should we cover next?
